name: Seacrete
description: Seacrete is a mineral substrate grown directly from seawater through low-voltage electrolysis — a technology first proposed by Wolf Hilbertz in the 1970s and popularized by Marshall T. Savage in 'The Millennial Project.' A metal frame submerged in seawater and charged with a weak electrical current causes dissolved minerals (primarily calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide) to precipitate and accrete on the frame, building up a limestone-like material over weeks to months. The longer the current runs, the thicker and stronger the structure becomes. In 2200, seacrete construction has scaled from Savage's original vision of floating ocean colonies to the primary building material of Old Harbor's above-water structures and the Lake Michigan platform communities.
properties: Self-healing — damage to the structure is repaired by continued electrolysis, the seawater fills cracks with new mineral deposits
Strengthens over time — unlike concrete which degrades, seacrete continues to accrete as long as current flows
Carbon-negative — the process pulls dissolved CO2 from water as carbonate
Supports marine life — the mineral surface encourages coral, algae, and shellfish colonization, making structures into artificial reefs
Low energy — requires only 1.2 volts DC, easily provided by solar panels or tidal generators
Compressive strength comparable to concrete (20-30 MPa) at maturity
Cannot be poured or shaped like concrete — must be grown on a frame, which limits architecture to the frame's geometry
Growth rate: approximately 2-5 cm per year in Lake Michigan's mineral-rich water
developers: Palladian Construction (licensed the process for Great Lakes application)
Old Harbor Community Builders (unlicensed, learned from Palladian's discarded research)
The Reef Collective (open-source seacrete farming cooperative)
applications: Old Harbor reconstruction — the drowned district's above-water structures are largely seacrete, grown on salvaged metal frames from flooded buildings
Lake Michigan platform foundations — the floating communities and relay stations use seacrete pontoons that strengthen with age
Breakwaters and sea walls — the Shelf's lakefront defenses include seacrete barriers that self-repair after storm damage
Artificial reef construction — environmental restoration projects grow seacrete reefs to rebuild Lake Michigan's collapsed ecosystem
Low-income housing foundations — the cheapest building material available, requiring only a metal frame, seawater, and electricity
Emergency infrastructure — after disasters, seacrete frames can be deployed in any body of water and grow structural material from nothing
tier_availability: Tier 1-3 (the material is free — seawater and electricity. The expertise to grow it properly is the expensive part.)
cost: Φ0.50/kg (material cost is near zero — you're paying for the frame and the electrician who sets up the current. Compare to Φ3/kg for standard concrete.)
story_hooks: Old Harbor's seacrete buildings are alive — the bioluminescent algae that colonizes them makes the walls glow, and an E.L.F. called Tidepool creates micro-ecosystems in the mineral pores

A Palladian Construction executive discovers that Old Harbor has been growing seacrete structures using a proprietary Palladian process — technically patent infringement, practically a community's survival

A seacrete structure that has been growing for 40 years is discovered to contain something unexpected in its mineral layers — the electrolysis process captured and preserved data from the flooded infrastructure beneath it, encoding information in the crystal structure of the accretion
